newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK consumer credit and M0.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK consumer credit and M0.

text.p: Following are a list of analysts' reactions to data showing British consumer credit rose 1.105 billion stg in May while M0 rose a provisional 6.3 percent year-on-year in June.

"Consumer credit is growing at a pretty frenetic pace. The fact that everybody is getting cheques from building societies is leaving them pretty relaxed about spending. The only question is how much of an interest rate rise and how much of a consumer tax rise we're going to see."

"The UK data are stronger than expected and are consistent with an overly robust trend in consumer spending. Both net lending and M0 growth came in above forecast, and strong headline levels are compounded by buoyant components. Hence within a one billion stg plus jump in consumer net lending, borrowing on credit card surged more than 300 million. This should be seen as indicative of a high level of consumer confidence which, with the building society handouts providing the funds to spend, is likely to translate into a potentially inflationary spurt in retail sales."

"A very consistent message we're getting. Not only was consumer credit very strong in May, the April figure was revised up substantially. Consumers are borrowing quite merrily. Much of this may be linked to anticipation of the building society windfalls but there is no getting away from the fact that consumers are spending freely. That message is a clear one for the Bank of England and the Chancellor on Wednesday."

"We were going for high figure of a billion anyway, so we are not unduly surprised, it fits in with the story of burgeoning consumer demand. It is a worry because we have such strong windfall gains from the building societies. It reinforces the need for further tightening policy, the question is whether it is monetary tightening or fiscal tightening. We should expect some tightening in the budget and that will take some of the edge of monetary policy, but we will nevertheless have a steady rise in interest rates throughout the year. It is an unwelcome development but not an altogether surprising one."
